concepts.name: shareIn/stateIn start strategies: Eagerly, Lazily and WhileSubscribed
Non-transitive R classes and resources from other modules
Google Play internal, closed and open testing tracks

questions.prompt: A ViewModel exposes `prices = ticker.shareIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, replay = 0)`. The ticker emits five prices before the screen starts collecting. What does the screen's collector get?

choices.text: All five earlier prices first, then each new price as it arrives later
Only the prices emitted after it subscribes; the first five are gone
Nothing at all, because `Eagerly` waits for a collector to appear
Only the newest of the five, then new ones, as a `StateFlow` would

questions.explanation: `SharingStarted.Eagerly` starts the upstream before the first subscriber appears, and any value beyond the `replay` count emitted with nobody subscribed is discarded. With `replay = 0` nothing is kept, so the late collector sees only later prices. Getting every value is what `Lazily` gives its first subscriber; getting the newest one would need `replay = 1`.

sources.title: shareIn
sources.claim: With Eagerly the upstream starts before the first subscriber and values emitted beyond the replay count are immediately discarded; Lazily starts on the first subscriber, which gets all values; WhileSubscribed starts on the first subscriber and stops when the last one disappears.

questions.prompt: The app module's code refers to `R.string.retry`, a string defined in `:core:ui`. After moving to AGP 8, that line no longer compiles, though the string still exists. Why?

choices.text: R8 removed the string, because only `:core:ui` code referred to it
`:core:ui` must now expose its strings with `api`, not `implementation`
A resource must now be declared in the app module before it can be packaged
Each module's `R` now holds only its own resources; use `:core:ui`'s `R`

questions.explanation: Since AGP 8.0, non-transitive R classes are the default: each module's `R` class contains only that module's own resources, not those of its dependencies. The string is still packaged; the app just has to name it through `:core:ui`'s `R` class (its namespace). R8 runs on release builds and can't break compilation, and `api` vs `implementation` controls classpath exposure, not what an `R` class contains.

sources.title: Optimize your build speed
sources.claim: Non-transitive R classes make each module's R class contain only references to its own resources, not its dependencies', which speeds up builds; this is the default in AGP 8.0.0 and higher.

questions.prompt: Before a production launch you want QA to get every build within minutes, then a beta for 1,500 invited users, then a public beta anyone can join. Which Google Play testing track fits each stage, and what limits or trade-offs come with each?

model_answer.summary: Internal testing for QA, closed testing for the invited beta and open testing for the public beta; each widens the audience but is slower and more visible.
key_points: Internal testing fits QA: up to 100 testers per app, invited by email, and a new bundle reaches them within minutes
Closed testing fits the invited beta: testers come from email lists or Google Groups (up to 2,000 users per list), and a release can take hours to become available
Open testing fits the public beta: anyone can find and join it on Google Play, and it is visible in search
Feedback from testers doesn't affect the public rating: test versions can't get public reviews, only private feedback

questions.explanation: The three tracks trade speed for reach. Internal testing is the fast lane for a small team and may skip the usual review, so it suits every CI build. Closed testing scales to invited groups, and open testing makes the beta public. A common mistake is to use open testing for QA builds, which exposes unfinished builds and waits for review.

sources.title: Set up an open, closed, or internal test
sources.claim: An internal test can have up to 100 testers per app and a new bundle becomes available within minutes; closed tests use email lists (up to 2,000 users each) or Google Groups and take hours to become available; open tests are visible on Google Play and anyone can join; testers can't leave public reviews and their feedback doesn't affect the public rating.

questions.prompt: Compare `SharingStarted.Eagerly`, `SharingStarted.Lazily` and `SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed()` for `shareIn`. When does each start and stop the upstream, and what does a subscriber that arrives late get?

model_answer.summary: Eagerly starts at once and never waits for subscribers, Lazily starts on the first subscriber and then runs forever, and WhileSubscribed runs only while someone collects; late subscribers get only the replay cache, then new values.
key_points: `Eagerly` starts the upstream immediately, before any subscriber, and values beyond the `replay` count emitted with no subscriber are discarded
`Lazily` starts the upstream when the first subscriber appears, so that subscriber gets every value, and keeps it running even after all subscribers leave
`WhileSubscribed()` starts on the first subscriber and stops when the last one disappears, keeping the replay cache
A late subscriber to any of them gets only the most recent `replay` values, then new emissions

questions.explanation: The strategy decides how long the expensive upstream (a socket, a database query) stays alive. `Lazily` is tempting because it never misses values for the first subscriber, but it keeps the upstream active forever. `WhileSubscribed` is the usual choice for UI state because it stops work when nobody is watching.

sources.title: shareIn
sources.claim: Eagerly starts before the first subscriber and discards values beyond replay; Lazily starts on the first subscriber, which gets all values, and stays active when subscribers disappear; WhileSubscribed stops when the last subscriber disappears, keeping the replay cache forever; later subscribers get the most recent replay values.

sources.title: StateFlow and SharedFlow
sources.claim: WhileSubscribed keeps the upstream producer active while there are active subscribers; Eagerly starts the producer immediately and Lazily starts after the first subscriber and keeps the flow active forever.

questions.prompt: Why does AGP 8.0 and later turn on non-transitive R classes by default?

choices.text: Each module's `R` lists only its own resources, so builds do less work
Resource IDs become `final` constants, so `when` branches can use them
It lets R8 rename every resource, which hides their names in the APK
Each module can then override any resource that a dependency defines

questions.explanation: With non-transitive R classes, a module's `R` class no longer repeats every resource of its dependencies, which avoids duplication and lets Gradle skip recompiling modules (compilation avoidance), so builds get faster. The same page recommends non-constant R classes, the opposite of `final` constants, also the default in AGP 8.0.

sources.title: Optimize your build speed
sources.claim: Non-transitive R classes ensure each module's R class only includes its own resources, giving faster builds and compilation avoidance by preventing resource duplication; non-constant R classes are also recommended and are the default in AGP 8.0.0 and higher.

questions.prompt: Five QA engineers must install every CI build from Google Play within minutes of upload. Which track fits best?

choices.text: Open testing, since anyone with the link can join it straight away
Closed testing with a Google Group, since its builds skip Play review
Internal testing, which serves up to 100 testers within minutes
A 1% production rollout, limited to the accounts of the QA team

questions.explanation: Internal testing is built for this: up to 100 testers per app, and a new bundle is available to them within minutes. Closed and open testing releases take hours to become available, and open testing is public. A staged production rollout picks a random share of real users; it can't be limited to chosen accounts.

sources.title: Set up an open, closed, or internal test
sources.claim: An internal test can have up to 100 testers per app and a new bundle becomes available to testers within minutes; closed and open tests take several hours to become available, and open tests are visible on Google Play.

questions.prompt: Before launch you want QA to get each build within minutes, then a beta for 1,500 invited users, then a public beta anyone can join. Which statements about Google Play's testing tracks are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Internal testing suits QA: up to 100 testers, and builds arrive within minutes
Testers' reviews of the open beta count toward the app's public star rating
Closed testing suits the invited beta, with email lists or Google Groups
Internal testing suits the invited beta too, as it allows 2,000 testers
Open testing suits the public beta: it's visible on Google Play to anyone

questions.explanation: Internal testing reaches up to 100 testers and a new build becomes available within minutes, so it fits QA but not 1,500 users. Closed testing uses email lists (up to 2,000 users each) or Google Groups, so it fits the invited beta, though a release can take hours to reach testers. Open testing is visible on Google Play and anyone can join, so it fits the public beta. Testers can't leave public reviews on test versions, and their feedback doesn't affect the public rating.

sources.title: Set up an open, closed, or internal test
sources.claim: Internal testing reaches up to 100 testers and becomes available within minutes; closed tests use email lists of up to 2,000 users each or Google Groups and can take several hours to become available; open tests are visible on Google Play and anyone can join; testers can't leave public reviews and their feedback doesn't affect the public rating.

questions.prompt: A repository exposes `upstream.shareIn(scope, started, replay = 1)`. Which statements about the `started` strategies are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: `Eagerly` starts the upstream even before the first subscriber appears
`WhileSubscribed()` clears the replay cache once the upstream is stopped
`Lazily` starts on the first subscriber and keeps running after all leave
A late subscriber to a `Lazily` flow gets every value emitted so far
`WhileSubscribed()` stops the upstream when the last subscriber leaves

questions.explanation: `Eagerly` starts the upstream at once, before any subscriber, discarding values beyond the replay count. `Lazily` starts when the first subscriber appears, so that one gets every value, and stays active even when all subscribers disappear. `WhileSubscribed()` starts on the first subscriber and stops when the last one disappears, keeping the replay cache forever. Later subscribers get only the most recent `replay` values (here one), then new ones.

sources.title: shareIn
sources.claim: `Eagerly` starts the upstream before the first subscriber; `Lazily` starts after the first subscriber, which gets all values, and stays active when all subscribers disappear, while later subscribers get only the most recent replay values; `WhileSubscribed` stops when the last subscriber disappears, keeping the replay cache forever.
